blocks.text: Acids and bases dissolved in water may or may not be completely dissociated. Many acids are weak electrolytes and ionise to an extent much less than 100 per cent. The value of Ka, the dissociation constant of an acid, is the quantitative measure of the strength of the acid. For an acid HA in water, HA + H2O gives H3O+ + A-, and Kc = [H3O+][A-] / ([HA][H2O]); taking the constant water concentration across, Kc [H2O] = [H3O+][A-] / [HA], and with Kc [H2O] = Ka: Ka = [H3O+][A-] / [HA]. This equation gives Ka for any acidic solution when the pH or [H+] and the initial concentration of the dissolved acid are known, and it also gives the equilibrium concentrations of H3O+ and A- when the initial concentration of HA and its Ka are known.

blocks.title: Acid strength from Ka
blocks.text: When Ka is less than 10^-3 the acid is weak; when Ka is between 1 and 10^-3 the acid is moderately strong; when Ka is greater than 1 the acid is strong.

blocks.caption: Ka values of some acids (Table 9.3, as printed)
rows: NH4+ gives H+ + NH3 (printed NH4 1 and NH5)

blocks.prompt: A vinegar sample is 0.837 M CH3COOH and its hydronium concentration is 3.86 x 10^-3 mol dm-3. Calculate Ka (Quick Check 9.3c).

items: Ka = Kc [H2O] = [H3O+][A-] / [HA] measures acid strength: Ka below 10^-3 weak, 1 to 10^-3 moderately strong, above 1 strong.
Table 9.3: HCl, HNO3 and H2SO4 very large; HF 6.7 x 10^-5, CH3COOH 1.85 x 10^-5, H2S 1.0 x 10^-7, NH4+ 5.7 x 10^-10, HCO3- 4.7 x 10^-12, H2O very weak.
